events.summary: STORY: Unionized workers at South Korea's Kakao staged a four-hour strike and rally on Wednesday.They demanded job security and changes to the tech firm's bonus system. Hundreds of workers wearing black T-shirts and holding white umbrellas walked out of Kakao's office in the morning.The union had told police as many as 1,200 members would join the rally.Local media reported the union plans a general strike for June 29 with all 5,000 members due to take part.Kakao operates South Korea's biggest messaging app by users, and employs about 6,000 people.The dispute comes with growing labor unrest in South Korea as tech firms score record earnings during the global AI boom.Samsung Electronics' union got ⁠a ​deal this month tying chip division bonuses to ​10.5% of operating profit.Kakao said last month it had failed to reach a wage deal with the union in government-mediated talks.The union wants reform to Kakao's compensation system.They argue executives have received higher bonus payments in recent years while other employees have seen limited benefits.Kakao previously said it turned down a union demand for profit-sharing, calling it unrealistic.The union refused to confirm details on the negotiation.Kakao said Wednesday its running a real-time system in response to the strike.It added management will keep talking with the union.
events.title: Kakao union stages four-hour strike and rally in South Korea over pay

events.summary: South Korea's Kakao Corp union said on Monday it will stage a four-hour strike ‌and rally in Pangyo on June 10, demanding job ‌security and reforms to a compensation system it says disproportionately rewards executives.  In a ​statement, the union said its core demands include halting restructuring such as divestments and spin-offs and improving what it called an "executive-centric pay system" that fuels job insecurity.  The move ⁠comes after government-mediated wage talks broke down last week, with Kakao rejecting union demands — including profit-sharing proposals — as unrealistic and "a big ​burden" on ​management as it prioritises investment ​and shareholder returns.
events.title: Union at South Korea's Kakao to hold partial strike on June 10

events.summary: South Korean tech firm Kakao Corp  said it has failed to ‌reach a pay deal with its union after ‌second-round negotiations mediated by the government on Wednesday.  Unionised workers at Kakao Corp and four affiliates, including headquarters, Kakao Pay ⁠Corp and Kakao Enterprise, previously voted to support a plan to go on strike.  The union has not confirmed ​how many ​of its members at ​Kakao Corp and four ‌affiliates would participate in a strike.
events.title: South Korea's Kakao says it fails to reach a pay deal with union

The author points out specific financial weaknesses for each, including poor net interest margins, underperforming earnings per share growth relative to revenue, and muted annual tangible book value growth compared to peers. This downturn is attributed to factors like the end of EV tax credits, manufacturers chasing higher margins through expensive vehicles, and consumers facing reduced purchasing power and record auto loan debt. The author suggests automakers' current strategies of prioritizing high-margin units and streamlining workforces may exacerbate the problem by creating more consumers unable to afford new vehicles.

However, with inflation at 3.8%, real home values declined for the eleventh consecutive month. Regional variations were significant, with Chicago leading at a 6.5% gain while Seattle experienced the steepest decline at 2.3%, and mortgage rates around 6.3% continued to constrain affordability.

events.summary: Lloyds Banking Group (LON:LLOY) saw its shares rise by 2.3% despite a cooldown in UK mortgage approvals and weakening business confidence, driven primarily by its ongoing share buyback program. Investors are weighing the impact of softer loan numbers against Lloyds' income outlook, buybacks, and return-on-tangible-equity targets.

events.summary: Mizuho Financial Group and Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group have significantly boosted foreign-currency bond sales by Japanese companies, reaching a record US$54 billion in the quarter ending June 30. This surge is driven by a depreciating yen and rising local interest rates, prompting Japanese firms to seek financing in overseas markets. Companies like Panasonic and Honda are also contributing to this trend as they look to fund large capital expenditures and overcome lacklustre demand for long-dated yen debt.

events.summary: Despite a headline inflation rate reduction, underlying core inflation in Australia increased, raising concerns for the RBA's interest rate decisions. However, interest rate expectations for an August hike have reduced, and Australian government bond yields continue to fall. While bonds are now considered fair value, equities, particularly technology stocks, appear expensive, with better opportunities in healthcare and consumer-related sectors.

events.summary: Star investor Eric Sprott views the recent decline in gold and silver prices as "short-term noise" driven by futures market volatility, rather than a weakening of fundamentals. He emphasizes the long-term upward trend for precious metals, supported by global macroeconomic conditions, particularly the loss of confidence in fiat currencies, strong physical demand from Asia, and central bank diversification. Sprott also highlights silver's dual role as a monetary asset and an industrially critical metal facing a growing supply deficit due to its use in renewable energy and AI.
